paras: The lynching of Lewis Davis took place early on September 23, 1888, when a masked mob broke into the jail at Steelville, Missouri, and hanged Davis, who was awaiting trial for the murder of farmer David Miller. He was hanged over the grave of Pat Wallace, lynched in the same county in 1886, a detail that headlined the coverage. Judge Bland ordered a special grand jury, but no report of its findings appears in the coverage.

In January 1888 a wire paragraph reported that the body of David Miller, a farmer near Cuba Junction, Mo., had been found with a bullet hole in the back of his head and $200 missing. Davis, a neighbor, was arrested and denied the charge, but "a party has been organized to lynch him."

A Globe-Democrat correspondent later wrote that Miller left home on January 2 to meet Davis and collect money owed him, carrying nearly $40. His body was found a week later near the farm of Davis's brother Elliott, shot in the head, the pockets turned out. Evidence before the coroner's jury pointed to Davis, and a Cuba dispatch said the bullet fitted his pistol. Indicted in March, Davis won a continuance; by September one key witness had died and another had left the state, and "the chance of conviction seemed remote."

After six months in the St. Louis jail, Davis was returned to Steelville for trial, and a jury was selected for Monday. On Saturday another jury acquitted Elbert Clonts of murdering his father, and both correspondents suggested the verdict led the mob to expect Davis to go free too.

About 2 a.m. on Sunday, masked men entered the town, posted guards at the streets and at Judge Bland's hotel, and ordered residents indoors at gunpoint. Deputy Sheriff R. P. Dunlap, sent to warn the judge, was seized and marched back to the jail, and the single guard on duty was overpowered. With sledges and chisels from a blacksmith shop, they spent about an hour cutting through the jail's iron doors.

Davis fought with pieces of a broken bedstead, and, according to the Globe-Democrat, asked his cellmates to have his brother bury him at home. The mob led him with a rope around his neck half a mile north of Steelville on the Cuba road and hanged him from an oak over Wallace's grave. He made no confession and told the mob he was innocent.

Judge Bland ordered a special grand jury and declared that all violators of the law must be punished. The Globe-Democrat correspondent wrote that the lynchers were heavily masked and that "not a single one could be identified." Reports noted that Davis came from "a family of high standing" and that his brother had twice been elected assessor. No report of arrests, indictments or grand jury findings against the mob was found.

The January paragraph ran in the Turner County Herald in Dakota and two Wyoming weeklies. Two separate dispatches carried the lynching. A Cuba report, partly relayed through Chicago, ran on September 24 and 25 in the San Antonio Daily Light and Alexandria Gazette as "Murderer Lynched," in the Washington Evening Star, and in the Richmond Dispatch. Its fullest version, in the Forrest City Times, carried the subhead "Brutal Work of a Mob" yet asserted there was "no doubt that Davis would have been convicted."

The Globe-Democrat letter from Midland was reprinted in the New York Sun on September 30 and condensed in the Barton County Democrat as "Murderer Hanged by a Mob Over the Grave of a Former Victim of Judge Lynch." Two Michigan weeklies printed a summary headed "Lewis Davis, Who Murdered His Friend and Neighbor, Hanged by Masked Men." Most papers treated Davis's guilt as settled; the Sun's text called him "the alfrighted murderer" while reporting his denials, and no report mentioned race.

The Cuba dispatch counted about forty masked men; the Globe-Democrat, thirty. The Barton County Democrat said the trial "was in progress," but the two detailed accounts agree it was to begin Monday. The January paragraph's $200 also differs from the later figure of nearly $40, and one summary named the dead man "David Mills."

bases: A masked mob broke into the county jail, took out Davis, who was held for trial on a murder charge, and hanged him (A4, A8, A9).

Thirty to forty masked men overpowered the jail guard and a deputy, took Davis from jail and hanged him (A4, A9, A10); they acted because of the murder charge against him, reportedly fearing an acquittal (A8, A9).

accounts.label: January wire paragraph
accounts.gist: Miller's body found in the doorway of an empty cabin six miles from Cuba Junction with $200 missing; Davis arrested and denying the charge, with a party organized to lynch him.

accounts.label: Cuba dispatch
accounts.gist: About forty masked men seized the deputy, cut down the jail door and hanged Davis over Wallace's grave; the bullet fitted his pistol and conviction was considered certain; the Clonts acquittal enraged the mob.

accounts.label: Globe-Democrat correspondent (Midland)
accounts.gist: Thirty masked men guarded the town and broke the jail doors over an hour while Davis fought with pieces of a bedstead; witnesses had died or left, conviction seemed remote, and the Clonts acquittal likely prompted the mob.

framing.detail: The Cuba dispatch ran as 'Murderer Lynched' and 'Taken From Jail and Lynched,' stressing that Davis fought desperately.
The Forrest City Times headed the fuller Cuba report 'Brutal Work of a Mob' yet asserted Davis would surely have been convicted.
The Globe-Democrat letter called Davis 'the alfrighted murderer' while reporting his denials and the weakness of the case, and noted the judge's promise to punish the mob.
The syndicated summary headed him 'Lewis Davis, Who Murdered His Friend and Neighbor,' stating the circumstantial evidence was strong.
